newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Europe's future security to be OSCE summit focus.
newsitem.headline: Europe's future security to be OSCE summit focus.

text.p: Russia hopes to win a commitment from American and European leaders at a summit in Lisbon next month to shape a new security model for Europe to remove risks of division between nations inside NATO and those outside.

Russia, uneasy over the planned eastward expansion of the Atlantic military alliance, wants the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to be the forum where defence, security and military matters concerning Europe can be discussed and deliberated.

"The Russians would like the OSCE to be at the top of a security umbrella...and remove the feeling of a vacuum among those states which have no hope of NATO membership in the next couple of decades," an OSCE official told Reuters on Monday.
"They want the OSCE to be the primary institution in the region for crisis prevention and management, committing states to avoid dividing lines in Europe," the official said.
The ambitious idea was being discussed at a review conference taking place in Vienna where the OSCE's decision-making permanent council is based.
Moscow wants the proposals to be adopted at the OSCE biannual summit in Lisbon on December 2 and 3 with a treaty ready for signing at the forum's next summit in 1998.
But Western diplomats said the Russian plan for a new security organisation was so complex that it was unlikely to win unanimous backing in Lisbon.
"That is not to say that the idea cannot be discussed beyond Lisbon," one Western diplomat said.
"But one thing is certain, NATO members are not going to put the actual question of expansion on the line...That is part of internal NATO policy," the diplomat said.

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are almost guaranteed a place in the first phase of expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), with Romania and Slovenia emerging as possible candidates.
Russia's plan for a security framework for the 21st century is one of several ideas floated in Vienna, but without Moscow's support other proposals were likely to be doomed.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, addressing the OSCE permanent council in September, said Europe, together with its partners in North America, had to grasp the chance to set up a new security structure, otherwise new lines of division based on military alliances would emerge across the continent.
He said the OSCE was uniquely positioned to be bolstered into Europe's main security body as it was the only European institution of which Moscow and Washington were members.
Hundreds of officials from the 53 OSCE member states and numerous non-governmental organisations were attending the Vienna review conference which ends on Friday.
The conference will draw up a series of draft documents on a range of issues, including minority and human rights, in preparation for the Lisbon summit.
OSCE officials said most European leaders, including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, French President Jacques Chirac and British Prime Minister John Major, were expected to attend.
It was unlikely, however, that U.S. President Bill Clinton would have time to travel to Portugal while he was busy setting up his new administration, a Western diplomat said.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from open heart surgery, was not expected but he may send Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin instead.
